title: SQL vs NoSQL
objectives: Relational for joins and transactions; NoSQL for flexible schema and massive horizontal scale.

cards.title: Choosing by access pattern
cards.body: SQL (Postgres, MySQL) gives schemas, joins and ACID. NoSQL families: key-value (DynamoDB), document (MongoDB), wide-column (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j). Choose by access pattern.

cards.title: Deciding between SQL and NoSQL
cards.body: List the queries first; joins and multi-row transactions point to SQL, a few huge key-based access patterns point to NoSQL, and the estimates confirm it.
steps: Joins or multi-row transactions? Lean SQL
A few huge key-based patterns? Consider NoSQL
Check the choice against the estimates

cards.title: Worked example: does one SQL primary fit?
cards.body: Assume: 10 million users, 20 orders each per year, 2 KB per order row with indexes; Peak 3,000 order writes per second during a sale.
steps: Storage per year = 200,000,000 × 2 KB = 400,000,000 KB, which is about 400 GB.
Five years of orders is about 2 TB: large, but within what one primary with replicas can hold on modern SSDs.
3,000 writes per second is within reach of one tuned primary with batching and good indexes; reads go to replicas and caches.
cards.note: A single relational primary plus read replicas fits this workload for years. Shard or move a specific table to NoSQL only when measured growth says one machine will not cope.

cards.title: Trap: NoSQL 'because it scales'
cards.body: Choosing NoSQL "because it scales" when the data is relational and modest in size.

questions.prompt: Which fits strongly relational data with multi-row transactions?

choices.label: Redis as the primary store
Cassandra
DynamoDB with single-item writes
PostgreSQL

questions.explanation: Joins and ACID transactions are what relational databases do best.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of NoSQL family and example is correct?

choices.label: Document: Neo4j
Graph: DynamoDB
Wide-column: Cassandra
Key-value: MongoDB

questions.explanation: Document: MongoDB; graph: Neo4j; key-value: DynamoDB.

questions.prompt: A team wants NoSQL “because it scales” for 50 GB of orders, customers and invoices with many joins. Best response?

choices.label: Agree: NoSQL is faster at any size
Shard SQL across 10 nodes from day one
Start with SQL: the data is relational and modest, and one node handles it
Use a graph database because there are relationships

questions.explanation: Choose by access pattern and size, not by slogan.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning for picking a store.

items.label: Ask: need huge write scale or a flexible shape?
Pick SQL or a NoSQL family

questions.explanation: Patterns first, then validate with numbers.

questions.prompt: Store for a ride app’s driver location pings.
constraints: Lookups by driver and time only

approaches.label: Wide-column store (Cassandra)
approaches.description: Partition by driver, sort by time

rationaleOptions.label: Cassandra adds multi-row ACID transactions
Write volume is beyond one SQL node
Access is by key, so joins are not needed

rationaleConflicts.r3: It does not; you give up joins and multi-row transactions for write scale.

questions.explanation: Massive writes with key-based reads fit wide-column stores.

flashcards.back: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
Access patterns, consistency needs, scale.

title: Types of NoSQL
objectives: Model for your queries: denormalise, pick partition and sort keys, avoid scatter-gather.

cards.title: Query-first data modelling
cards.body: In DynamoDB/Cassandra, design tables per query. Partition key spreads data; clustering/sort key orders within a partition. Duplicate data instead of joining.

cards.title: Modelling a table around its queries
cards.body: Pick a partition key that spreads load, a sort key that orders rows for the query, and duplicate data so each read hits one partition.

cards.title: Worked example: sizing a chat partition
cards.body: Assume: Average message row 300 bytes; A busy group sends 2,000 messages a day; Target partition under 100 MB.
steps: Bytes per day = 2,000 × 300 = 600,000 bytes, about 0.6 MB.
A conversation-only partition key would cross the target in under six months for busy groups and keep growing.
Bucketing by month, (conversation_id, month), caps a busy partition at about 0.6 × 31 ≈ 18.6 MB.
cards.note: Partition by conversation and month: newest-first reads touch one or two buckets, and no partition grows without bound.

cards.title: Trap: modelling NoSQL like SQL
cards.body: Modelling NoSQL like SQL with normalised tables and app-side joins.

cards.title: The four families
cards.body: Key-value (DynamoDB, Redis): get by key, simplest and fastest. Document (MongoDB): JSON-like records with nested fields. Wide-column (Cassandra): a partition key plus sorted rows, built for huge write volume. Graph (Neo4j): nodes and edges for questions like friends-of-friends.

questions.prompt: In Cassandra, what does the clustering (sort) key control?

choices.label: The order of rows inside a partition
The replication factor
Which node stores the partition
Which secondary index is used

questions.explanation: The partition key places data; the clustering key orders it.

questions.prompt: Which query fits a graph database best?

choices.label: Append a million sensor readings a second
Fetch a product document with nested specs
Get a session by id
Friends of friends who live in Pune

questions.explanation: Multi-hop relationship queries are what graph stores are for.

questions.prompt: Order the NoSQL modelling steps.

items.label: Serve each query from one partition

questions.explanation: Design tables per query.

questions.prompt: A Cassandra schema copies SQL: normalised tables joined in the app. Result?

choices.label: Several round trips per page and scatter-gather reads
Joins run on the server automatically
Stronger consistency
Less storage and faster reads

questions.explanation: Wide-column stores have no joins; duplicate data per query instead.

questions.prompt: Chat messages are read as “latest 50 in a conversation”. Partition key and sort key?

choices.label: Partition by sender_id, sort by receiver_id
Partition by message time, sort by conversation_id
Partition by conversation_id, sort by message time
Partition by day, sort by message id

questions.explanation: One partition per conversation, already in time order. Partitioning by day would make today’s partition hot.

flashcards.back: Design tables around queries.
Partition picks the node; sort orders rows in it.

title: Indexing: B-Tree & LSM
objectives: Indexes (B-trees, hash, inverted) speed reads at the cost of writes and storage.

cards.title: What an index buys and costs
cards.body: A B-tree index turns a full scan into a log-time lookup. Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule. Each index slows inserts and updates.

cards.title: From full scan to index lookup
cards.body: Without an index the database scans every row; a B-tree turns that into a few page reads, paid for with extra work on every write.

cards.title: Worked example: how few levels a B-tree needs
cards.body: Assume: Fan-out of 200 keys per page; 500 million rows.
steps: One level covers 200 keys; two levels cover 200 × 200 = 40,000.
Four levels cover 8,000,000 × 200 = 1,600,000,000, which is more than 500 million.
So any row is at most four page reads away, and with the root and second level cached, about two reads from disk.
cards.note: A B-tree over half a billion rows is only four levels deep, which is why an indexed lookup takes milliseconds while a full scan of 500 million rows takes minutes.

cards.title: Trap: indexing every column
cards.body: Indexing every column. Writes slow down and the planner may still ignore them.

cards.title: LSM trees
cards.body: LSM-tree stores (Cassandra, RocksDB) buffer writes in memory and flush sorted files to disk, merging them later (compaction). Writes are sequential and fast; a read may check several files, helped by Bloom filters. B-trees update pages in place: steadier reads, slower heavy writes.

questions.prompt: An index on (city, created_at). Which query uses it best?

choices.label: WHERE city = 'Pune' AND created_at > '2026-01-01'
WHERE status = 'paid'
WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01'
WHERE created_at = '2026-01-01' OR city = 'Pune'

questions.explanation: Leftmost prefix: the query must constrain city first.

questions.prompt: What is the cost of five more indexes on a busy table?

choices.label: Reads get slower because the planner has more choices
The table can no longer be sharded across machines
Nothing once they are built; indexes only cost at creation
Every insert and update must also update five more structures

questions.explanation: Indexes trade write cost and storage for faster reads.

questions.prompt: Which workload favours an LSM-tree store over a B-tree?

choices.label: Small tables that fit in memory
Very high write volume, such as event logging
Complex joins across many tables
Mostly point reads on rarely changing data

questions.explanation: LSM trees turn writes into sequential appends.

questions.prompt: Order the story of adding an index.

items.label: Writes pay to maintain the index

questions.explanation: Faster reads, slower writes.

questions.prompt: A B-tree with fan-out 100 indexes 100M rows. About how many levels deep is it?
questions.explanation: Design implication: four levels means a lookup touches about four pages, and the top levels usually stay cached in memory, so an indexed lookup in 100M rows costs about one disk read.

flashcards.back: Composite index usable only from its first column(s).
Slower writes, extra storage.

title: Normalization vs Denormalization
objectives: Explain what normalization buys you
Recognise when to denormalize for reads
Name the cost of keeping copies in sync

cards.title: Normalize first
cards.body: Normalization stores each fact once: a customer’s address lives in one row, orders point to it by ID. Updates touch one place, so data cannot disagree with itself.

cards.title: Denormalize for hot reads
cards.body: If the order page must show product name and seller name, a normalized schema joins three tables on every view. At 5,000 order-page views a second during a sale, copying those names into the order row makes each view a single-row read; the cost is that a seller rename must now update every one of their order rows.

cards.title: Read path, before and after
cards.body: The normalized page joins three tables on every view; the denormalized page reads one row, at the cost of keeping the copies in sync.

cards.title: Trap: denormalising up front
cards.body: Denormalizing everything up front. Start normalized, measure the hot query, then denormalize that path and decide how copies stay in sync (same transaction, events, or accepted staleness).

questions.prompt: An order history page joins orders, products and sellers on every view and is now the slowest query. Most reasonable first change?

choices.label: Copy product and seller names into those order rows
Move all the data to a document store instead
Drop the foreign keys so the joins run faster
Denormalise every table in the schema at once

questions.explanation: Fix the measured hot path and keep the rest normalised; the copies cost a little on rare renames. Moving everything to a document store, or denormalising the whole schema, is a rewrite for one query, and foreign keys are checked on writes; they do not slow down reads that join.

questions.prompt: What is the main cost of copying the seller name into 10M order rows?

choices.label: Reads then need more joins to fetch each order
The database loses its ACID guarantees for orders
A seller rename must update many rows, or the copies go stale
Orders can no longer be indexed by seller or date

questions.explanation: With 10M copies, one seller rename updates every row that seller has, possibly millions, so it belongs in a background job. Reads need fewer joins, not more, and ACID guarantees and indexing are unaffected.

questions.prompt: A wallet app shows the user’s balance on 6 different screens. Which data should stay in one normalised place?

choices.label: The display name on a cached profile card
The balance used to approve payments
The merchant name on past transactions
The product name printed on old invoices

questions.explanation: The balance decides whether a payment goes through, so two copies that disagree mean approving money that is not there; keep one authoritative row, updated in a transaction, and have the screens read it. Merchant names on past transactions and product names on invoices are snapshots that should not change, and a cached display name can be a little stale.

questions.prompt: Order the recommended process.

items.label: Decide how copies stay in sync

questions.explanation: Denormalise late and on purpose.

questions.prompt: Show product names on order history: copy or join?
constraints: Order history is the hottest page
Old orders should show the name at purchase time

approaches.label: Copy the name into the order row

rationaleOptions.label: Keeping the name as it was at purchase is actually wanted
The hottest page becomes a one-row read
Copied names can never go stale

rationaleConflicts.r3: They can. Here staleness is acceptable, even wanted, but you still decide how renames propagate.

questions.explanation: Copying suits read-heavy pages whose data rarely changes.

flashcards.back: Update anomalies: the same fact stored in two places disagreeing.
Faster reads for extra writes and the work of keeping copies in sync.
After a measured hot read path, with a clear sync strategy.

title: Transactions & ACID
objectives: Explain each ACID property with an example
Show how atomicity protects a transfer
Spot code that needs a transaction

cards.title: ACID
cards.body: Atomicity: all of a transaction’s writes happen or none do. Consistency: constraints hold before and after. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other’s half-done work. Durability: once committed, the change survives a crash.

cards.title: Atomicity in practice
cards.body: A transfer debits one account and credits another. If the server crashes between the two, atomicity rolls the debit back, so money never disappears in between.

cards.title: A transfer transaction
cards.body: Both balance changes sit inside one transaction, so a crash before COMMIT leaves neither applied.
steps: Write the change to the log

cards.title: Durability
cards.body: Commit returns only after the change is in the write-ahead log on disk, and with synchronous replication on a replica too. After a crash the database replays the log.

cards.title: Trap: two auto-committed writes
cards.body: Running two related writes as separate auto-committed statements. A crash between them leaves half a change. Put them in one transaction, and keep it short.

questions.prompt: Inside one transaction, the server crashes after debiting A but before crediting B. After restart?

choices.label: The database asks the user what to do
Neither change is visible: the transaction rolled back
Both changes are applied because the debit started
A is debited and B is not

questions.explanation: All or nothing.

questions.prompt: Which ACID property guarantees a committed order survives a power cut?

choices.label: Atomicity
Consistency
Durability
Isolation

questions.explanation: Committed means written to the log.

questions.prompt: A CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint stops a transfer from overdrawing. Which property is that?

choices.label: Consistency
Durability
Isolation
Atomicity

questions.explanation: Constraints that hold before and after every transaction.

questions.prompt: Order a transfer transaction.
questions.explanation: The log write is what makes commit durable.

questions.prompt: Two related writes run as separate auto-committed statements. What can go wrong?

choices.label: Reads become slower
A crash between them leaves only half the change
The second write is always rejected
They deadlock every time

questions.explanation: One transaction makes them atomic.

flashcards.front: Inside one transaction, the server crashes after debiting A but before crediting B. After restart?
flashcards.back: Neither change is visible: the transaction rolled back. All or nothing.

flashcards.front: Which ACID property guarantees a committed order survives a power cut?
flashcards.back: Durability. Committed means written to the log.

flashcards.front: A CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint stops a transfer from overdrawing. Which property is that?
flashcards.back: Consistency. Constraints that hold before and after every transaction.

flashcards.front: Two related writes run as separate auto-committed statements. What can go wrong?
flashcards.back: A crash between them leaves only half the change. One transaction makes them atomic.

title: Isolation Levels
objectives: Name the anomalies each isolation level prevents
Pick a level for money vs analytics
Explain why stronger isolation costs throughput

cards.title: What isolation protects
cards.body: Concurrent transactions can see each other’s half-done work. Isolation levels decide which anomalies you accept: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms and write skew.

cards.title: The levels
cards.body: Read committed: no dirty reads (Postgres default). Repeatable read / snapshot: a stable view for the whole transaction. Serializable: as if transactions ran one at a time, at the cost of more aborts and retries.

cards.title: Two doctors go off call
cards.body: Under snapshot isolation both transactions see two doctors on call and both commit; serializable isolation detects the conflict and aborts one.
steps: Snapshot isolation lets both commit: 0 on call

cards.title: Trap: assuming serializable
cards.body: Assuming the default level is serializable. Most databases default to read committed, so check what you are getting before relying on it for money.

questions.prompt: Which anomaly does READ COMMITTED prevent?

choices.label: Phantoms
Non-repeatable reads
Dirty reads
Write skew

questions.explanation: It only hides uncommitted data.

questions.prompt: Two on-call doctors each check “someone else is on call” and remove themselves, under snapshot isolation. Result?

choices.label: One blocks until the other commits, so one stays on call
Snapshot isolation always serialises them
Both commit and nobody is on call (write skew)
Both are rolled back automatically

questions.explanation: Each saw a consistent snapshot; together they broke the rule.

questions.prompt: Order these isolation levels from weakest to strongest.
questions.explanation: Stronger levels allow fewer anomalies and cause more aborts.

questions.prompt: Isolation for a booking rule that spans rows (a party of 4 must sit together), which one conditional UPDATE cannot check.
constraints: Many users race for the same seats

approaches.label: Serializable, with retries on abort
approaches.description: As if one at a time

rationaleOptions.label: Aborted transactions can be retried safely
Serializable rejects interleavings such as write skew
Snapshot isolation prevents write skew

rationaleConflicts.r3: Snapshot gives a stable view but still allows write skew, as in the doctors example.

questions.explanation: Pay for serializable where an invariant spans rows. For a single seat, a conditional UPDATE (or a unique constraint) under read committed is enough, as the lesson shows.

questions.prompt: A Postgres app relies on serializable behaviour without setting it. What does it actually get?

choices.label: Read committed, the default
Snapshot isolation for writes only
Read uncommitted
Serializable, the default

questions.explanation: Check the level before relying on it for money.

flashcards.back: Read committed.

flashcards.front: What anomaly can snapshot isolation still allow?
flashcards.back: Write skew.
More aborts and retries, lower throughput under contention.

title: BASE & Eventual Consistency
objectives: Explain what BASE trades away
State what eventual consistency guarantees and what it does not
Choose a conflict resolution strategy

cards.title: BASE
cards.body: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent. Instead of locking replicas together, the system keeps answering and lets replicas catch up in the background. Reads may be stale for a while.

cards.title: What “eventual” guarantees
cards.body: If writes stop, all replicas converge to the same value. It does not say how soon, and it does not stop a user seeing an older value after a newer one.

cards.title: A like on a post
cards.body: The nearest replica accepts the like and replies immediately; other replicas learn about it a moment later and converge.

cards.title: Resolving conflicts
cards.body: Two replicas may accept conflicting writes. Last-write-wins keeps the later timestamp and silently drops the other; counters and sets can merge instead (CRDTs); some apps keep both versions and ask the user.

cards.title: Trap: eventual consistency for money
cards.body: Using eventual consistency for a wallet balance. Two replicas can both approve a spend. Keep money and inventory on strongly consistent paths.

questions.prompt: Under eventual consistency, what is guaranteed?

choices.label: Reads never go backwards in time
Every read returns the latest write
Replicas converge within 100 ms
If writes stop, replicas converge to the same value

questions.explanation: Convergence, with no time bound.

questions.prompt: Which feature suits BASE-style eventual consistency?

choices.label: Wallet debits
Like counts on posts
Seats for a sold-out show
Claiming a unique username

questions.explanation: A briefly stale like count harms nobody.

questions.prompt: Two replicas accept different edits to a profile bio. With last-write-wins, what happens?

choices.label: The edit with the later timestamp is kept and the other is silently lost
The user is asked to choose between the two edits on next login
Both edits are merged character by character into one bio
Both writes are rejected until the replicas agree on one value

questions.explanation: LWW is simple but drops data.

questions.prompt: Order an eventually consistent write.
questions.explanation: The reply comes before replication finishes.

questions.prompt: Count video views at a million increments a second.

approaches.label: Per-replica counters merged in the background (a CRDT counter)

rationaleOptions.label: This gives exact real-time counts everywhere
Per-replica counters merge without coordination
A slightly stale count is acceptable

rationaleConflicts.r3: Counts converge later; viewers may see an older number for a while.

questions.explanation: Mergeable counters scale writes when exactness can wait.

flashcards.front: Under eventual consistency, what is guaranteed?
flashcards.back: If writes stop, replicas converge to the same value. Convergence, with no time bound.

flashcards.front: Which feature suits BASE-style eventual consistency?
flashcards.back: Like counts on posts. A briefly stale like count harms nobody.

flashcards.front: Two replicas accept different edits to a profile bio. With last-write-wins, what happens?
flashcards.back: The edit with the later timestamp is kept and the other is silently lost. LWW is simple but drops data.

title: Replication
objectives: Copies of data on multiple nodes for availability and read scaling; sync vs async trade-offs.

cards.title: Leaders, followers and lag
cards.body: Leader-follower: writes to leader, replicas serve reads with lag. Sync replication = no loss but slower; async = fast but may lose recent writes on failover. Multi-leader adds conflict resolution.

cards.title: A write replicating to followers
cards.body: The leader records the change in its log and ships it to replicas, which apply it in order; reads from replicas can lag behind.

cards.title: Worked example: how much data asynchronous failover can lose
cards.body: Assume: Leader takes 2,000 writes per second; Replication lag 300 ms at the moment of failure.
steps: Those 600 writes were acknowledged to clients but exist only on the dead leader.

With semi-synchronous replication to one follower, every acknowledged write has already reached that follower’s log (received, though not necessarily applied), so failing over to it loses no acknowledged writes, at the cost of about one network round trip per commit (often under 1 ms in the same zone).
cards.note: Asynchronous replication can lose roughly 'write rate × lag' acknowledged writes on failover; size that number before choosing.

cards.title: Trap: reading your write from a lagging replica
cards.body: Reading your own write from a lagging replica — the user sees their order "missing". Use read-your-writes routing.

questions.prompt: A user posts a review, refreshes, and it is missing. Likely cause?

choices.label: A database constraint rejected it silently
The read went to a replica that had not caught up yet
The user’s session expired
The leader lost the write

questions.explanation: Route a user’s reads to the leader briefly after they write.

questions.prompt: What does asynchronous replication risk?

choices.label: Split brain on every write
Losing the latest writes if the leader fails before shipping them
Slower writes, because the leader waits for replicas
Replicas refusing reads

questions.explanation: Async is fast because it does not wait.

questions.prompt: What new problem does multi-leader replication bring?

choices.label: Conflicting writes on different leaders must be resolved
Every write must take a global lock first
Reads can no longer scale across replicas
Replicas can no longer lag behind leaders

questions.explanation: Two leaders can accept the same key at once.

questions.prompt: Order leader-follower replication.
questions.explanation: Replica reads lag by the shipping time.

questions.prompt: Replication for a payments ledger with a replica in another zone.
constraints: No committed payment may be lost
A few ms of extra write latency is fine

rationaleOptions.label: A commit is on two machines before success is returned
Synchronous replication makes writes faster
Losing a committed payment on failover is unacceptable

rationaleConflicts.r3: It makes them slower; the leader waits for the replica’s acknowledgement.

questions.explanation: Pay latency for durability where money is involved.

flashcards.back: Route a user’s reads to leader shortly after their writes.
Losing recent writes on failover.

title: Quorums N/R/W
objectives: Use R + W > N to reason about reading the latest write
Tune N, R, W for read- or write-heavy loads
Explain sloppy quorums and hinted handoff

cards.title: Quorums in one line
cards.body: With N replicas, a write waits for W acknowledgements and a read asks R replicas. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps the latest write set, so at least one replica returns the newest value.

cards.title: Tuning
cards.body: N=3, W=2, R=2 is the balanced default. W=1, R=3 makes writes fast and reads slow; W=3, R=1 does the opposite but any replica outage blocks writes.

cards.title: A quorum read
cards.body: With N = 3 and R = 2, a read that touches two replicas sees at least one with the latest write, and read repair fixes the stale one.
steps: Client reads key from 2 of 3 replicas
Replica A has v5, replica B has v4
Read repair updates B to v5

cards.title: Trap: quorum is not linearizable
cards.body: Treating R + W > N as full linearizability. Sloppy quorums, clock-based conflict resolution and concurrent writes can still return surprising results.

questions.prompt: N=5, W=3, R=3. Can a normal read miss the latest successful write?

choices.label: No: every read set overlaps the write set by at least one replica
Yes, but only when one of the five replicas is down
Yes: for overlap R + W must exceed 2N, which is 10
Yes, unless the read waits for all five replicas

questions.prompt: N = 5 replicas and W = 3. What is the smallest R that guarantees overlap?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: with R = 3 and W = 3 out of N = 5, any read set and write set share at least one replica (3 + 3 > 5). Lower R makes reads faster but can miss the latest write.

questions.prompt: N=3. Writes must be fast; reads can be slower. Which setting?
questions.explanation: W=1 acknowledges quickly; R=3 restores overlap.

questions.prompt: Order a quorum read with read repair.

items.label: Replica A has v5, B has v4
Read repair updates B to v5

questions.explanation: Reads heal stale replicas as a side effect.

questions.prompt: Is R + W > N enough for linearizability?

choices.label: No: you also need R = N, and then it is always enough
No: sloppy quorums and concurrent writes can still give surprising results
Yes, always: overlapping quorums are linearizable
Yes, as long as N is odd so there are no ties

questions.explanation: Overlap is not the same as linearizability.

flashcards.back: R + W > N.
Strong write durability, but any replica outage blocks writes.
Updating stale replicas discovered during a read.

title: Partitioning & Sharding
objectives: Split data across nodes by key — range, hash or directory — to scale writes and storage.

cards.title: Choosing a shard key
cards.body: Pick a shard key with high cardinality and even access. Hash sharding spreads load; range sharding helps range queries but risks hotspots. Cross-shard joins and transactions get hard.

cards.title: Routing a row to its shard
cards.body: Hash the shard key, map the hash to a shard (mod N or a ring), send the query there, and rebalance as data grows.

cards.title: Worked example: how many shards?
cards.body: Assume: 8 TB of data, growing 2 TB per year; Each shard comfortably holds 1 TB with headroom; Peak writes 40,000 per second; one shard handles 5,000.
steps: Shards for storage in 2 years = (8 plus 4) ÷ 1 = 12.
Start with, say, 64 logical shards placed on 12 machines, so later growth moves logical shards instead of re-splitting data.
cards.note: Size shards by the larger of storage and write needs, add growth headroom, and use many logical shards so rebalancing is a move, not a rewrite.

cards.title: Trap: a skewed shard key
cards.body: Choosing a low-cardinality or skewed shard key (country, city, or celebrity user_id).

questions.prompt: Which shard key most likely creates a hotspot for an India-first app?

choices.label: country
hashed user_id
hashed order_id
hashed device_id

questions.explanation: Nearly every row has the same country.

questions.prompt: After sharding by user_id, what gets harder?

choices.label: Adding an index within a shard
Looking up one user’s data
Backing up one shard
Queries and transactions that span many users

questions.explanation: Single-user work stays on one shard; cross-user work does not.

questions.prompt: Range sharding an event log by timestamp. Main risk?

choices.label: Keys spread too evenly
All new writes land on the newest shard
It requires consistent hashing
Range queries become impossible

questions.explanation: Time ranges concentrate current writes.

questions.prompt: Order the sharding setup.

items.label: Map the hash to a shard

questions.explanation: Rebalancing is part of the plan from day one.

questions.prompt: Data is sharded by city. The Mumbai shard is at 95% CPU while others idle. Click the hot spot.
questions.explanation: A skewed key concentrates load. Shard by a high-cardinality key instead.

flashcards.back: High cardinality, even distribution, matches access pattern.
Hotspots on recent/popular ranges.

title: Consistent Hashing
objectives: Map keys and nodes onto a ring so adding a node moves only ~1/N of keys.

cards.title: Rings instead of mod N
cards.body: With hash mod N, changing N remaps nearly every key. On a hash ring each key goes to the next node clockwise; virtual nodes even out load.

cards.title: Adding a node to a hash ring
cards.body: Keys walk clockwise to the first node; a new node takes over one arc, so only the keys in that arc move.

cards.title: Worked example: keys moved when a cache cluster grows
cards.body: Assume: 100 million cached keys; Cluster grows from 10 to 11 nodes.
steps: With hash mod n, a key stays only if hash mod 10 equals hash mod 11, which happens for about 1 in 11 keys.
So about 10 ÷ 11 of keys move: 100,000,000 × 10 ÷ 11 ≈ 91 million cache misses.
With consistent hashing, about 1 ÷ 11 of keys move: roughly 9.1 million.
Consistent hashing moves about one tenth as many keys as mod-n in this case.
cards.note: Adding one node to a mod-n cache empties almost the whole cache and can stampede the database; consistent hashing moves only the new node's fair share.

cards.title: Trap: no virtual nodes
cards.body: Forgetting virtual nodes — a few physical nodes get uneven arcs and become hot.

questions.prompt: With consistent hashing on 10 equal nodes, adding one moves roughly what share of keys?

choices.label: About 1/11
About 10/11
About half
None

questions.explanation: Only the arc the new node takes over moves.

questions.prompt: A ring has 4 equal nodes. A 5th joins with an equal share. What percentage of keys move?
questions.workedAnswer: 1/5 = 20% of keys move to the new node.
questions.explanation: Design implication: only about a fifth of keys move, compared with roughly 80% under hash mod N, which is why caches use consistent hashing: adding a node doesn't wipe most of the cache.

questions.prompt: Why not place keys with hash(key) mod N?

choices.label: It needs a coordinator for each lookup
Changing N remaps almost every key
It cannot handle string keys
Mod is slow to compute

questions.explanation: Adding one server would invalidate most of the cache.

questions.prompt: Why use virtual nodes?

choices.label: To even out each server’s share of the ring
To make replication unnecessary
To avoid hashing keys
To store more data per key

questions.explanation: Many small arcs per server average out uneven placement.

questions.prompt: Order a consistent-hashing lookup and a scale-out.

items.label: First node found owns the key
A new node takes over one arc

questions.explanation: Only keys in the new node’s arc move.

flashcards.back: Even out load across physical nodes.
Changing N remaps almost all keys.

title: CAP
objectives: During a network partition you choose consistency or availability; otherwise you trade latency vs consistency (PACELC).

cards.title: The choice during a partition
cards.body: CAP: under a partition (P), a system either rejects some requests to stay consistent (CP) or answers possibly-stale data (AP). Consistency models range from strong (linearizable) to eventual.

cards.title: What happens when the network splits
cards.body: During a partition each side must either refuse requests to stay consistent (CP) or answer with possibly stale data (AP), then reconcile after healing.

cards.title: Worked example: how much a partition costs each choice
cards.body: Assume: Partition lasts 2 minutes; Side B serves 30% of 10,000 requests per second.
steps: Requests on side B during the partition = 10,000 × 0.3 = 3,000 per second.
CP: up to 360,000 requests fail or wait on side B, but no one sees inconsistent data.
AP: those 360,000 requests succeed, and some may read stale data or create conflicts to resolve later.
cards.note: CAP is a per-operation business choice: count who is affected and what a wrong answer costs.

cards.title: Trap: 'pick two of three'
cards.body: Saying "pick two of three" as if you can drop P. Partitions happen; the real choice is C vs A during one.

questions.prompt: During a partition, which should favour consistency over availability?

choices.label: Like counts
Product recommendations
View counters
Seat inventory for a sold-out concert

questions.explanation: Selling the same seat twice is worse than a brief error.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with “pick two of C, A and P”?

choices.label: Partitions happen anyway; the real choice is C or A during one
You can have all three with enough replicas
P is optional on a fast network
It only applies to SQL databases

questions.explanation: You cannot opt out of partitions.

questions.prompt: Order the CAP story.

items.label: Choose: reject some requests (CP) or serve possibly stale data (AP)

questions.explanation: The choice only bites during the partition.

questions.prompt: Posture for a social “like” counter during partitions.

approaches.label: AP: keep accepting likes, reconcile later

rationaleOptions.label: AP guarantees every user sees the same count
Staying available keeps the app usable
A briefly wrong count harms nobody

rationaleConflicts.r3: AP serves possibly stale data; users can see different counts until the partition heals.

questions.explanation: Choose AP where staleness is cheap.

questions.prompt: During a partition, a CP system will:

choices.label: Promote a leader on both sides so every request succeeds
Accept writes on both sides and merge conflicts automatically
Return possibly stale data so that every node stays available
Reject or delay some requests rather than return stale data

questions.explanation: Consistency first, at the cost of availability.

flashcards.back: Choose consistency (reject) or availability (maybe stale).
Else (no partition): latency vs consistency trade-off.

title: PACELC
objectives: State PACELC and how it extends CAP
Label common databases PA/EL or PC/EC
Pick latency or consistency per feature

cards.title: PACELC in one line
cards.body: If there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, in normal operation, choose Latency or Consistency.

cards.title: The everyday trade-off
cards.body: Partitions are rare, but latency hits every request. A strongly consistent read may need a quorum or a trip to the leader in another region; a local replica answers faster but may be behind.

cards.title: Labelling systems
cards.body: Dynamo-style stores such as Cassandra default to PA/EL: stay up and answer fast. Spanner-like databases are PC/EC: always consistent, paying latency for it.

cards.title: One read, two choices
cards.body: Even with no partition, each read chooses between a fast local answer that may be stale and a slower answer from the leader.
steps: Client in Mumbai reads a price
EL: local replica answers in about 2 ms, maybe stale
EC: read goes to the leader in Singapore, about 60 ms
Pick per feature: catalogue EL, checkout EC

cards.title: Trap: stopping at CAP
cards.body: Explaining CAP and stopping there. Most of the time there is no partition, and the real question is how much latency you pay for consistency.

questions.prompt: What does PACELC add to CAP?

choices.label: A durability guarantee for acknowledged writes
A way to avoid network partitions altogether
A third choice besides C and A during partitions
A latency-versus-consistency choice when there is no partition

questions.explanation: The E/L half covers normal operation.

questions.prompt: Cassandra with default settings is usually labelled:

choices.label: PA/EL
PA/EC
PC/EC
PC/EL

questions.explanation: Available under partition, low latency otherwise.

questions.prompt: Product catalogue browsing in normal operation. Which read?

choices.label: Block reads until replication is fully idle
The local replica (EL): a slightly old description is fine
Always the leader, even in another region
A quorum read across three regions each time

questions.explanation: Spend latency on consistency only where staleness hurts.

questions.prompt: A strong read from Mumbai goes to a leader in Singapore (60 ms); a local replica answers in 2 ms. How many ms extra does each strong read cost?
questions.explanation: Design implication: 58 ms extra on every strong read adds up across a page, so pay it only where staleness matters (checkout, balances) and serve the rest from the local replica.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning for one read.

items.label: Client in Mumbai reads a price
Option EL: local replica, fast, maybe stale
Option EC: leader in Singapore, slower, fresh

questions.explanation: The answer differs by feature.

flashcards.front: What does PACELC add to CAP?
flashcards.back: A latency-versus-consistency choice when there is no partition. The E/L half covers normal operation.

flashcards.front: Cassandra with default settings is usually labelled:
flashcards.back: PA/EL. Available under partition, low latency otherwise.

flashcards.front: Product catalogue browsing in normal operation. Which read?
flashcards.back: The local replica (EL): a slightly old description is fine. Spend latency on consistency only where staleness hurts.

sources.title: Abadi, “Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design”, IEEE Computer 45(2), 2012

title: Consistency Models
objectives: Distinguish strong, read-your-writes and eventual consistency
Pick a consistency level per feature, not per system
Explain what a user sees under each model

cards.title: Consistency is per feature
cards.body: One app can need several models. A UPI balance needs strong consistency; a like counter can be eventual; a user editing their profile should at least see their own write.

cards.title: The ladder
cards.body: Strong (linearizable): every read sees the latest write. Read-your-writes: you always see your own updates. Monotonic reads: you never go back in time. Eventual: replicas converge if writes stop.

cards.title: Read after a write
cards.body: A lagging replica can show a user their old profile right after they changed it; read-your-writes routes their reads to the primary for a short time.
steps: Eventual: next read may show old profile
Read-your-writes: route this user’s reads to primary briefly

cards.title: Trap: strong consistency everywhere
cards.body: Choosing strong consistency everywhere. It costs latency (cross-replica coordination) and availability during partitions. Spend it only where stale data causes real harm.

questions.prompt: A user changes their display name, refreshes, and sees the old one because the read hit a lagging replica. Cheapest guarantee that fixes it?

choices.label: Monotonic reads
Eventual consistency
Linearizability for every user
Read-your-writes

questions.explanation: Only the writer needs to see the change immediately.

questions.prompt: Which feature most needs strong consistency?

choices.label: A UPI balance check before a debit
A creator’s follower count
Like counts on a viral post
Trending hashtags this hour

questions.explanation: Stale balances cause real harm.

questions.prompt: A user refreshes and sees 10 comments, then 8, then 10 again. Which guarantee is missing?

choices.label: Monotonic reads
Read-your-writes
Atomicity
Durability

questions.explanation: Reads hit replicas at different lag, so time appears to go backwards.

questions.prompt: Order the read-after-write fix.

items.label: User updates their profile on the primary
Next read may show the old profile
Route this user’s reads to the primary briefly

questions.explanation: A targeted fix instead of strong consistency everywhere.

questions.prompt: Consistency for profile edits.
constraints: The editor must see the change
Others can see it a little later

rationaleOptions.label: Strong consistency everywhere has no real cost
The editor must see their own change
Other users can see the update a moment later

rationaleConflicts.r3: It costs coordination latency on every read and availability during partitions.

questions.explanation: Spend consistency only where stale data hurts.

flashcards.back: A user always sees their own updates, even if others may see them later.
Counters, feeds, recommendations: places where brief staleness is harmless.
Higher latency and lower availability during partitions.

title: Choosing the Right DB
objectives: Scale in steps: optimise queries → cache → read replicas → vertical → shard.

cards.title: Exhaust the simple steps before sharding
cards.body: Many systems can go a long way without sharding. First fix slow queries and indexes, add caching and read replicas, then scale vertically, and finally partition by a well-chosen key.

cards.title: The scaling ladder for a database
cards.body: Fix queries and indexes, add a cache, add read replicas, move to a bigger instance, and shard only when writes or data size demand it.

cards.title: Worked example: when does a single primary run out?
cards.body: Assume: Primary handles about 10,000 simple writes per second; Product grows writes 2× per year from 1,500 per second today.
steps: Year 3: 6,000 × 2 = 12,000 per second, which exceeds about 10,000.
So there are roughly two to three years before writes force sharding, plenty of time to plan rather than shard on day one.
cards.note: Project growth against measured capacity to decide when to shard, and say that timeline out loud in an interview.

cards.title: Trap: sharding at 100 QPS
cards.body: Proposing sharding at 100 QPS. Sharding is expensive to undo; justify it with write volume or data size.

cards.title: Match the store to the access pattern
cards.body: Relational for orders, payments and anything with joins and transactions. Key-value for sessions and carts by id. Document for flexible product data. Wide-column for huge append-heavy writes. A search engine for full text. Object storage for files. Many systems use a few of these.

questions.prompt: A database sits at 80% CPU from repeated identical reads. First step?

choices.label: Shard the database
Switch to NoSQL
Cache those reads
Go multi-region

questions.explanation: Cheapest fix that removes the load.

questions.prompt: Order a sensible database scaling path.
questions.explanation: Sharding is last because it is hard to undo.

questions.prompt: When is sharding justified?

choices.label: When reads are slow and the tables still have no indexes
When writes or data size exceed one primary, after the cheaper steps
When the team adopts microservices and wants one DB each
As soon as traffic passes about 100 queries per second

questions.explanation: Justify it with write volume or data size.

questions.prompt: Where should user-uploaded profile photos live?

choices.label: In Elasticsearch, next to the profile
Object storage, with the URL saved in the database
In BLOB columns in the users table
In Redis, used as the primary store

questions.explanation: Files go to object storage; metadata to the database.

questions.prompt: Stores for a food-delivery app: orders and payments, menu search, session carts.

approaches.label: Postgres for everything, searching with LIKE
Postgres for orders, a search engine for menus, Redis for carts

rationaleOptions.label: One database is always the simplest to scale
Full-text search needs a search engine
Orders need transactions

rationaleConflicts.r3: A single store forced to serve every pattern gets slow somewhere; match patterns but keep the count small.

questions.explanation: Match stores to patterns.

flashcards.back: After indexing, caching, replicas and vertical scaling are exhausted.
Read throughput, not write throughput.

title: Message Queues
objectives: Queues decouple producers from consumers, absorb spikes and enable async work.

cards.title: Decoupling with a queue
cards.body: Producers enqueue; workers consume at their own pace. Queues buffer bursts, isolate failures and allow retries. Use them when the caller does not need the result immediately.

cards.title: A job through a queue
cards.body: The producer enqueues and returns; workers pull at their own pace and ack on success, so failures are retried instead of lost.

cards.title: Worked example: sizing workers for a burst
cards.body: Assume: Sale spike: 50,000 receipt jobs per minute for 10 minutes; Each job takes 200 ms; one worker does 5 jobs per second; Acceptable backlog: cleared within 20 minutes of the spike starting.
steps: To finish within 20 minutes (1,200 seconds) needs 500,000 ÷ 1,200 ≈ 417 jobs per second.
Workers needed = 417 ÷ 5 ≈ 84; to keep pace with the peak instead would need 833 ÷ 5 ≈ 167.
cards.note: The queue lets about 84 workers handle a peak that would otherwise need about 167, at the cost of receipts arriving up to 20 minutes late.

cards.title: Trap: queues for synchronous work
cards.body: Putting synchronous user-facing work behind a queue and then polling for the result.

cards.title: Poison messages
cards.body: A malformed message that crashes the consumer will be redelivered forever and block the queue. After a few failed attempts, move it to a dead-letter queue and alert someone.

questions.prompt: Which task is best moved to a queue?

choices.label: Showing the cart total on checkout
Validating a coupon before showing the price
Checking the password at login
Sending the order-confirmation email

questions.explanation: The user does not need the email’s result to continue.

questions.prompt: A flash sale brings 10× normal orders for 5 minutes; the invoice service handles 1×. What does a queue give you?

choices.label: Orders are rejected until the spike ends
Invoices are generated 10× faster
Orders are accepted now and invoices catch up after the spike
Nothing: the queue forwards at the same rate

questions.explanation: Queues absorb bursts; consumers work at their own pace.

questions.prompt: One malformed message crashes the consumer every time and blocks the queue. Fix?

choices.label: Retry it forever with no delay between attempts
Add more consumers until one of them succeeds
After a few failed attempts, move it to a dead-letter queue and alert
Purge the whole queue and ask producers to resend

questions.explanation: Park poison messages so the rest can flow.

questions.prompt: Order a queued job.
questions.explanation: Unacked jobs come back.

questions.prompt: During a spike, 6,000 jobs/min arrive and workers finish 4,000/min. How large is the backlog after 15 minutes?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the backlog only drains once arrivals drop below 4,000/min. At 2,000/min below capacity, clearing 30,000 jobs takes another 15 minutes, so add workers or shed load.

flashcards.back: Decoupling and load levelling.
Consumer confirms processing so message is removed.

title: Kafka
objectives: Pub/sub fans one event to many subscribers; Kafka is a partitioned, replayable log.

cards.title: Partitions, ordering and replay
cards.body: Kafka topics are split into partitions; order is guaranteed per partition. Consumer groups share partitions. Messages are retained so consumers can replay.

cards.title: An event through a Kafka topic
cards.body: The producer keys the event to a partition; the log retains it, and each consumer group reads it independently at its own offset.

cards.title: Worked example: choosing a partition count
cards.body: Assume: Peak 60,000 events per second; One consumer instance processes 2,500 events per second; Plan for 2× growth.
steps: Since one partition is read by at most one consumer in a group, the topic needs at least 48 partitions.
Choose a round number such as 64 to allow headroom; increasing partitions later changes which partition a key maps to.
cards.note: Partition count caps consumer parallelism, so size it for future peak throughput divided by per-consumer throughput, with headroom.

cards.title: Trap: expecting global ordering
cards.body: Expecting global ordering in Kafka. Ordering is per partition — key by order_id to keep one order’s events in sequence.

questions.prompt: How do you keep all events for one order in sequence?

choices.label: Add timestamps and sort in each consumer
Rely on Kafka’s ordering across partitions
Use order_id as the message key so they share a partition
Use one partition per consumer

questions.explanation: Ordering holds only within a partition.

questions.prompt: A topic has 6 partitions and a consumer group runs 8 consumers. What happens?

choices.label: The group refuses to start
Six consumers get one partition each; two sit idle
Every message goes to all 8
Kafka splits the partitions into 8

questions.explanation: A partition is read by one consumer per group.

questions.prompt: A bug corrupted a downstream table for the last two hours. How does Kafka help?

choices.label: It cannot: messages are deleted once consumed
Restart the producer to resend
Reset the consumer’s offset and replay the retained messages
Add partitions

questions.explanation: Retention makes the log replayable.

questions.prompt: Analytics and billing both need every order event. How?

choices.label: The producer calls each service directly
One consumer group shared by both services
Billing forwards each event to analytics
Two consumer groups, each reading the whole topic

questions.explanation: Groups are independent subscribers.

questions.prompt: Order an event’s path through Kafka.

items.label: Producer sends an event with a key
Event is appended to the retained log

questions.explanation: Each group tracks its own offset.

flashcards.back: Per partition only.

flashcards.front: Max parallel consumers in a group?
flashcards.back: Number of partitions.

title: Pub/Sub & Fan-out
objectives: Explain publish/subscribe and when to use it
Compare fan-out on write vs fan-out on read
Handle celebrity accounts in a feed

cards.title: Pub/sub decouples producers
cards.body: A publisher emits an event once (OrderPlaced); any number of subscribers (email, analytics, inventory) consume it independently. Adding a consumer does not change the producer.

cards.title: Fan-out on write vs read
cards.body: Fan-out on write pushes a new post into every follower’s feed at post time: fast reads, expensive writes. Fan-out on read assembles the feed when it is opened: cheap writes, slower reads.

cards.title: Posting with a hybrid feed
cards.body: Normal posts are pushed into followers' feeds when written; celebrity posts are skipped at write time and merged in when a feed is read.
steps: Workers push into normal followers’ feeds
Celebrity posts skipped at write time
Feed read merges celebrity posts on demand

cards.title: Trap: fan-out on write for celebrities
cards.body: Fan-out on write for everyone. A cricketer with 50 million followers turns one post into 50 million writes. Hybrid feeds treat high-follower accounts differently.

questions.prompt: An account with 50M followers posts. Why is pure fan-out on write a problem?

choices.label: Followers of celebrities cannot read feeds
One post becomes 50M feed writes
Pub/sub cannot deliver to more than 1M subscribers
Normal users’ reads get slower

questions.explanation: Write cost grows with follower count.

questions.prompt: Order service publishes OrderPlaced. Analytics wants it too. What changes in the order service?

choices.label: Publish a second event type for analytics
Add a direct call to analytics after each order
Write orders into analytics’ database too
Nothing: analytics subscribes to the topic

questions.explanation: Publishers do not know their subscribers.

questions.prompt: Fan-out on read means:

choices.label: The feed is assembled when the user opens it
Followers poll the poster’s phone
Only celebrities’ posts are stored
Posts are pushed into followers’ feeds at post time

questions.explanation: Cheap writes, slower reads.

questions.prompt: Order a post in a hybrid feed.

items.label: Workers push it into normal followers’ feeds
Celebrity posts are skipped at write time
Feed reads merge celebrity posts on demand

questions.explanation: Two paths by follower count.

questions.prompt: Feed strategy when most users have 200 followers but a few have 50M.

approaches.label: Hybrid: write fan-out for normal users, read-time merge for celebrities

rationaleOptions.label: Fan-out on read for everyone keeps every feed fast
Normal posts are precomputed, so most reads are fast
Celebrity posts merged at read time avoid millions of writes

rationaleConflicts.r3: Each open would gather posts from hundreds of followees; slow for the common case.

questions.explanation: Treat the long tail and the giants differently.

flashcards.back: Producers from consumers: new subscribers need no producer changes.

flashcards.front: Fan-out on write is good for?
flashcards.back: Fast feed reads for accounts with modest follower counts.
Skip write fan-out for them and merge their posts at read time.

title: Delivery Semantics
objectives: Compare at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once
Explain where duplicates come from
Make retries safe with idempotency and backoff

cards.title: Three guarantees
cards.body: At-most-once: send and forget; a crash can lose a message but never duplicates it. At-least-once: retry until acknowledged; nothing is lost but duplicates happen. Exactly-once: each message affects the result once, which in practice means at-least-once delivery plus idempotent or transactional processing.

cards.title: Where duplicates come from
cards.body: A consumer processes a message, then crashes before committing its offset. On restart it reads the message again. Producers also resend after a lost acknowledgement.

cards.title: An at-least-once consumer
cards.body: If the consumer crashes after processing but before committing its offset, the message comes back; an idempotent write makes the replay harmless.
steps: Idempotent write makes the replay harmless

cards.title: Retries with backoff
cards.body: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter. Immediate retries from thousands of clients turn a blip into a thundering herd; jitter spreads them out.

cards.title: Trap: promising exactly-once
cards.body: Promising exactly-once delivery over a network. Delivery can only be at-least-once; you get exactly-once effects by making processing idempotent.

questions.prompt: Which guarantee can lose a message but never duplicates it?

choices.label: At-most-once
At-least-once
Exactly-once
At-least-once with retries

questions.explanation: No retries means no duplicates, and no recovery.

questions.prompt: A consumer handles 1,000 messages/s and commits offsets every 5 seconds. It crashes just before a commit. About how many messages are replayed?
questions.explanation: Design implication: up to 5,000 messages will be processed twice after the crash, so the consumer's writes must be idempotent. Committing more often shrinks the replay but adds overhead.

questions.prompt: Why add jitter to retries?

choices.label: To guarantee exactly-once delivery of every message
So clients do not all retry at the same moment after an outage
To keep the retried messages in their original order
To make each individual retry complete more quickly

questions.explanation: Synchronised retries hit a recovering service all at once.

questions.prompt: Order the guarantees from weakest to strongest.
questions.explanation: Each step adds work: retries, then idempotency.

questions.prompt: Delivery for payment settlement events.
constraints: A duplicate settlement would pay twice

approaches.label: At-least-once with idempotent processing
approaches.description: Retry, and dedupe by settlement id

rationaleOptions.label: Idempotent processing makes duplicates harmless
No settlement may be lost
At-most-once avoids duplicates, so it is safest for money

rationaleConflicts.r3: It avoids duplicates by risking loss; a lost settlement is just as bad.

questions.explanation: Exactly-once effects come from at-least-once plus idempotency.

flashcards.front: Which guarantee can lose a message but never duplicates it?
flashcards.back: At-most-once. No retries means no duplicates, and no recovery.
So clients do not all retry at the same moment after an outage. Synchronised retries hit a recovering service all at once.

title: Idempotency
objectives: Explain why retries cause duplicates
Design an idempotency key flow
Apply it to payments and message consumers

cards.title: Retries create duplicates
cards.body: Networks time out after the server already did the work. The client retries, and without protection a UPI payment is charged twice. At-least-once queues redeliver the same way.

cards.title: Idempotency keys
cards.body: The client sends a unique key (Idempotency-Key header). The server stores key → result. A retry with the same key returns the stored result instead of repeating the action.

cards.title: A retried payment
cards.body: The server stores the idempotency key with the result, so a retry after a lost response gets the stored answer instead of a second charge.
steps: Client sends POST /pay with key K
Server finds K, returns stored success

cards.title: Trap: check, then write
cards.body: Checking for the key and then writing in two separate steps. Two concurrent retries can both pass the check. Make the key insert and the action atomic, for example with a unique constraint.

cards.title: Naturally idempotent operations
cards.body: Setting a value (status = shipped) is idempotent: doing it twice leaves the same result. Adding or appending (balance += 100) is not. Turn the second kind into the first by recording a key or checking a version.

questions.prompt: A payment request timed out on the client, but the server had already charged the card. The client retries. What prevents a double charge?

choices.label: An idempotency key: the server returns the stored result
A longer client timeout
Retrying faster
Exactly-once delivery from the network

questions.explanation: The retry is recognised and answered from storage.

questions.prompt: Two identical retries arrive in the same millisecond. Which design is safe?

choices.label: Keep keys in each server’s memory
Accept both and reconcile at month end
Check whether the key exists, then charge, in two steps
Insert the key under a unique constraint in the same transaction as the charge

questions.explanation: Check-then-act races; an atomic insert does not.

questions.prompt: Order a retried payment with an idempotency key.

items.label: Client sends POST /pay with key K
Server charges and stores K → success
Response is lost; client times out
Server finds K and returns the stored success

questions.explanation: The second request never charges.

questions.prompt: Which operation is naturally idempotent?

choices.label: Add ₹100 to the wallet balance
Set the delivery address to “12 MG Road”
Increment the post’s view count
Append a comment to the thread

questions.explanation: Setting a value twice leaves the same state.

questions.prompt: You keep idempotency keys for 24 hours. 2M payments a day, about 100 bytes per stored key and result. Storage needed, in MB?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 200 MB fits comfortably in memory or a small table, so keeping idempotency keys for a full day is cheap. Retention is a correctness choice, not a storage problem.

flashcards.front: What does an idempotency key do?
flashcards.back: Lets the server return the stored result for a retried request instead of repeating it.
At-least-once delivery means the same message can arrive twice.

flashcards.front: How do you stop two concurrent retries both running?
flashcards.back: Make the key insert atomic, e.g. a unique constraint in the same transaction.
